title: The last words
hookLine: "decay is inherent in all component things; work out your salvation with diligence" (DN 16, Rhys Davids)

lines: WHAT WOULD YOUR LAST WORDS BE?
THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.
cards: What would you say, if you knew they were your last words? Some well-known last words are funny, some are grand, and some were polished by whoever wrote them down.
It's deep in the night at Kusinara, between the sal trees. The monks are gathered around. Ananda is there.
Subhadda has been ordained. And the Buddha has a few things left to say. First, practical things.

When I'm gone, he tells Ananda, don't think you have no teacher. The teaching and the discipline I've given you will be your teacher. Then he asks the monks, three times, if anyone has any doubt left about the teaching.

teach.h: DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL THINGS.
teach.b: Then come the last words. In the 1881 translation by T. W.
Rhys Davids: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Everything put together comes apart, so keep going, with care.
The Pali word at the heart of it is appamada: heedfulness, carefulness, not letting yourself drift. A modern rendering puts it: strive on with diligence. Not a dramatic promise.
Not a claim about himself. The same two things he had taught all along, compressed into one breath: things end, so practice.
Then he passes through the stages of deep meditation, up and back down and up again, and from the fourth, the text says, he passes away.
Today's word names that: parinibbana, complete nibbana, the full going-out of an awakened one at death.

Buddhist traditions understand that ending in more than one way, and the Buddha himself refused to describe it in ordinary terms of existing or not existing. The earth trembles. Ananda speaks a short, shaken verse.
In Theravada countries, the festival of Vesak remembers this night together with the birth and the awakening, on one full-moon day.
Look back at this week of last days. The old cart that still rolled. Be your own island.
Vesali, lovely, and the elephant look.
Cunda's meal, and no one to blame. Rest at Kusinara. Subhadda, and still time.
And today, the last words. The whole life comes down to a line you could carry in your pocket.

how: In Theravada countries Vesak remembers the parinibbana together with the birth and awakening, East Asian traditions keep Nirvana Day, and the last words on heedfulness are often recited and quoted.

o: a chant that monks sing before they eat
the full going-out of an awakened one at death
a harvest festival held in the villages each year

games.q: what's inside the last words — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha named a person to be the teacher after him
he said the teaching and the discipline would be their teacher.
he asked three times if anyone had a doubt left
his last words were about things ending, and practicing with care
"decay is inherent in all component things! work out your salvation with diligence!"

games.q: you have minutes left, and your students are gathered around you. what do you say last?
o: a summary of your own achievements.
that all things end, so keep practicing with care.
games.why: things put together come apart; strive on with care. the same thing he had taught all along, in one breath.

practice: Sit in silence, with no instruction except the last one he gave. Let everything that arises in you arise, and everything that passes, pass; if your mind drifts, come back, gently, with care. Things end.

wordCard.voice: Parinibbana. Complete nibbana: the final passing of an awakened one, at Kusinara, after the last words.

orig.note: Pali: complete nibbana, the final passing of an awakened one. Sanskrit parinirvāṇa.

carryVoice: Your line: strive on with care. His whole teaching, in one breath. Day eighty-four, complete.

sources.q: Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!
